subject: E6C0C39827F843698AC33F901392B995
introduction: “Not a single thing reaches the limit of perfection immediately upon coming into existence, but grows and develops gradually.” The guide begins with seeds, seasons and embryos, turns to the idea that one divine bounty is received by each thing “according to its capacity”, and then applies both to religion: laws are revealed and changed as peoples become able to bear them, and a Faith, like Christ’s twelve disciples, begins small and grows slowly. The parables of Jesus are the nearest company, the blade and ear, the mustard seed, the leaven, the sower, the patient fig-dresser, with James’s husbandman and the Qur’an’s stages of the embryo. For revelation fitted to capacity there are “ye cannot bear them now”, Paul’s milk before meat and his law as schoolmaster, Jesus on what Moses allowed “because of the hardness of your hearts”, and the Qur’an’s own verse on abrogation. Mencius tells the best story against impatience, the farmer who pulled his corn to help it grow. Wordsworth’s “bliss was it in that dawn” remembers the opposite hope, and Darwin’s closing sentence shows gradual change admired in nature itself.
questions: Mencius’s farmer “helped” his corn by pulling it. Where, in bringing up children, in a community’s life or in one’s own, is that mistake made?
Readings 13 to 25 say the same sun shines on all and the difference lies in capacity. Reading 25 says capacity must be developed. Is capacity a fact about a person or a task for them?

Jesus says Moses permitted divorce “because of the hardness of your hearts”. Reading 32 explains the Qur’an’s marriage law similarly. What does this way of reading scripture assume about the purpose of a law?
If laws are fitted to an age’s capacity, how can anyone know that a time has come for a change?
The fig-dresser asks for one more year. When is patience with slow growth wisdom, and when is it an excuse?

outside.why: Nothing reaches perfection the moment it exists. The seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
A special time to plant, to grow, to harvest. To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted.
The creation of your souls is like what grows in the earth. The reading speaks with the Qur’an: Allah hath caused you to grow as a growth from the earth.

God lets a tree grow a long time before it is perfect; take the lesson. Mencius tells of a man of Song who, grieved that his corn was not longer, pulled it up to help it, and went home to say he had been helping the corn to grow. His son ran to look, and it was all withered.
The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.
God could raise all things to maturity in the twinkling of an eye, and does not. One day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
Nothing in nature rests; all things progress or lose ground. Longfellow: to act, that each to-morrow find us farther than to-day.
The embryo passes through forms and conditions until maturity. The Qur’an recites them: from dust, then from a drop of seed, then from a clot, then from a little lump of flesh.
Noah, in the Qur’an, puts it to his people as a reason for awe: when He created you by divers stages?

The spirit has other signs in childhood, adolescence and maturity. Jaques counts seven ages, and ends them in second childishness and mere oblivion. The reading describes the same life as a rising line. What does each leave out?
When I was a child, I spake as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
Each kingdom holds potentialities that must be cultivated. Shelley’s figure for what a thing holds before it unfolds: the first acorn, which contained all oaks potentially.
Each created being has its own excellence. Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
The sun shines with one radiance on all. He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.
Grace is like rain, taking the shape of what it falls on. The Qur’an: neighbouring tracts, vineyards and date-palms, watered with one water; and We have made some of them to excel others in fruit.
Every created thing is a sign of God, according to its capacity. The heavens declare the glory of God; day unto day uttereth speech.
In each world He appears according to that world’s capacity. He spake the word unto them, as they were able to hear it.
Realities appear in proportion to receptivity. We have this treasure in earthen vessels.
One sun, differing capacities. One sowing and four soils: the wayside, stony places, thorns, good ground.
Light appears in each object according to its capacity. To every man according to his several ability.
One sun, and one mineral stays a stone while another becomes a gem. The widow’s oil flowed while there were vessels to fill: there is not a vessel more. And the oil stayed.

Capacity must be developed to receive. Paul speaks of vessels of gold and of earth, and adds that a man may purge himself to become a vessel unto honour. Is capacity given or made? How do readings 23 to 25 answer?

Whatever is created must reach its perfection, unless prevented. A fig tree is three years barren, and the dresser pleads: let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it. How long is growth to be waited for?
The Pen has been mindful of people’s weakness. I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it.
Some ordinances are deferred because their time has not come. Neither do men put new wine into old bottles.
Changed conditions are the cause of the abrogation of laws. The Qur’an: nothing of Our revelation do We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, but We bring one better or the like thereof.
When Moses came the world had developed capacity for those laws. Paul: the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ.
Polygamy could not be forbidden at once among the Arabs. Jesus on the Mosaic permission of divorce: Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you; but from the beginning it was not so.
How little the world of yesterday resembles today’s. Burke: a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
Spiritual advancement is like the early dawn. The path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.

Wordsworth remembered a dawn of another sort, the first days of the French Revolution: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive. That hope was for everything at once, and it turned to terror within four years. What do the readings say to the wish for sudden transformation?
Gradually what is latent will appear. Precept upon precept; line upon line; here a little, and there a little.

The Law of God spreads like sunrise over the horizons. Darwin closes his book on slow change with the same pleasure in it: from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved. Does the gradualness he found in nature support the readings’ analogy, or is it a different thing?
What Christ established did not yield rapid results. The kingdom is like leaven hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
However good the seed and strong the sower, growth cannot be forced. I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
Twelve hearts, and it seemed so limited. For who hath despised the day of small things?
Eleven disciples at the crucifixion, and look at the result. The least of all seeds becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches.
Peace will not come at once after a declaration. The vision is yet for an appointed time: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come.
A downpour begins with a few drops. The Dhammapada on the inward work: as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.
The bounty is now a seed hidden in the earth. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.

Self-consciousness arose gradually, at no definite point. Aristotle: nature proceeds little by little from things lifeless to animal life, so that it is impossible to determine the exact line of demarcation.

shortfall: Readings 12 to 26 restate one idea, that one bounty is received according to capacity, a dozen times with the sun and its mirrors, and readings 35 to 46 and 49 to 53 repeat the image of the seed; each group was given a few companions and no reading a forced one.
